1.pericope_label: Look to the rock: Abraham, the comforted wilderness, and a righteousness that outlasts the heavens

schools.summary: Read the opening argument as evidence: Israel's improbable origin is itself the ground for believing in its restoration, the address may be to the nations rather than to Israel, and the vanishing heavens are resolved into atoms while the promise stands.
Take following after righteousness as the pursuit of a righteousness lying outside oneself, and list the ordinary channels through which the promised comfort is actually delivered.

Set the scheme of the whole chapter out first, weigh the manuscripts where they bear on who is addressed and how wide the word for righteousness reaches, and keep the loss of the heavens to their present state and use.
Turn the rock and the pit into a doctrine of the first birth, and read the description of God's people by their knowledge, their judgment and the law written in their hearts.

debates.question: Who is addressed as my people and my nation?

positions.view: Israel, the Jews as a peculiar people
the Gentiles, since several manuscripts read the plurals, ye peoples and ye nations, and God nowhere else calls his people my nation
God's special people, whether Jews or Gentiles

debates.question: What is the righteousness that is near?

positions.view: the righteousness of Christ, wrought out, revealed and applied
the word covering justice, truth, faithfulness, goodness, mercy, deliverance and salvation together, and meaning here the faithful keeping of a promise
judgment first and conversion after it, the far countries at last trusting the arm that struck them

debates.question: How do the inhabitants of the earth die?

positions.view: vanishing into nothingness, or on a rival rendering dying like gnats, a third comparison beside the smoke and the garment
passing away only in respect of their present state and properties, the substance not destroyed

outliers.reading: Alone reads the quarry and the pit as a lesson in natural birth rather than national history, setting beside Ur and the Egyptian slave-gangs the hardness of the rock any man is hewn from, and bidding those now advanced remember how low they began.

themes: Hearken to me, ye that follow after righteousness, ye that seek the Lord: look unto the rock whence ye are hewn, and to the hole of the pit whence ye are digged.
Look unto Abraham your father, and unto Sarah that bare you: for I called him alone, and blessed him, and increased him.

For the Lord shall comfort Zion: he will comfort all her waste places; and he will make her wilderness like Eden, and her desert like the garden of the Lord; joy and gladness shall be found therein, thanksgiving, and the voice of melody.
Hearken unto me, my people; and give ear unto me, O my nation: for a law shall proceed from me, and I will make my judgment to rest for a light of the people.
My righteousness is near; my salvation is gone forth, and mine arms shall judge the people; the isles shall wait upon me, and on mine arm shall they trust.

Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look upon the earth beneath: for the heavens shall vanish away like smoke, and the earth shall wax old like a garment, and they that dwell therein shall die in like manner: but my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness shall not be abolished.
Hearken unto me, ye that know righteousness, the people in whose heart is my law; fear ye not the reproach of men, neither be ye afraid of their revilings.
For the moth shall eat them up like a garment, and the worm shall eat them like wool: but my righteousness shall be for ever, and my salvation from generation to generation.

9.pericope_label: Awake, arm of the Lord: Rahab cut in pieces, and the Comforter who answers

schools.summary: Handle the apostrophe as a critical problem: four candidates for the speaker, a repeated verse that is either self-quotation or citation, an oppressor identified with the Babylonian monarchy, and an address spoken to Israel in its ideal rather than to the Servant.

Read the cry as the church's prayer through the prophet, addressed to the Father or to Christ, and the doubled pronoun of the answer as granting more than was asked, the Comforter himself instead of bare power.
Identify the figures and correct the text: Rahab for Egypt and the dragon for Pharaoh, a rescuer marching at speed rather than a hastening captive, and stretch out the heavens read for plant them.

Plead precedent and promise together, since past experience supports faith and may be urged in prayer, and note that God takes the work of comfort into his own hands because ministers cannot reach the heart.

debates.question: Who speaks the cry Awake, awake?

positions.view: the redeemed and ideal Israel, though the loftiness of the poetry may transcend the distinction between that, the Servant, the prophet and God self-communing
the prophet, or rather the church through him, addressing either the Father or Christ, and certainly not Jerusalem or Zion as some versions have it
the church, addressing an arm that stands for Christ or for God himself

debates.question: Where does the promise of the returning redeemed come from?

positions.view: it repeats an earlier chapter, either the prophet quoting himself or a later writer quoting him, and the charge of interpolation rests on no adequate ground
the repetition is a tool for correcting the text, the collation recovering two verbs and exposing a letter misread as the ending of the word before
it continues the prayer rather than answering it, though it may also be read as the answer
it is the answer: God did these things and means to do the like again
the church, or the prophet, or Christ as the great Prophet
the people, since God's word is said to be put in their mouths and not only in the prophets'
Israel contemplated in its ideal, neither the Servant directly nor a misplaced fragment, that ideal being filled only by the Servant

outliers.reading: Alone goes outside Scripture for a parallel to the cutting of Rahab, quoting through Cheyne an Egyptian invocation from the Book of the Dead that hails the sun god as one who cut the scorner in pieces and strangled the evil serpent.

themes: Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the Lord; awake, as in the ancient days, in the generations of old. Art thou not it that hath cut Rahab, and wounded the dragon?
Art thou not it which hath dried the sea, the waters of the great deep; that hath made the depths of the sea a way for the ransomed to pass over?

Therefore the redeemed of the Lord shall return, and come with singing unto Zion; and everlasting joy shall be upon their head: they shall obtain gladness and joy; and sorrow and mourning shall flee away.
I, even I, am he that comforteth you: who art thou, that thou shouldest be afraid of a man that shall die, and of the son of man which shall be made as grass;

And forgettest the Lord thy maker, that hath stretched forth the heavens, and laid the foundations of the earth; and hast feared continually every day because of the fury of the oppressor, as if he were ready to destroy? and where is the fury of the oppressor?
The captive exile hasteneth that he may be loosed, and that he should not die in the pit, nor that his bread should fail.
But I am the Lord thy God, that divided the sea, whose waves roared: The Lord of hosts is his name.
And I have put my words in thy mouth, and I have covered thee in the shadow of mine hand, that I may plant the heavens, and lay the foundations of the earth, and say unto Zion, Thou art my people.

17.pericope_label: Awake, Jerusalem: the cup of trembling drained and handed to her oppressors

schools.summary: Set the second awake against the first, the one opening a promise and the other a ruin, and read the details soberly: the goblet drained, the sons like corpses in the open places, an antelope in the net, and the rare plural title standing beside the name.

Hear the summons as a call out of death itself and the doubled title as security, the Lord of all who can do everything and the covenant God who does what he promised, with Babylon's fate falling at last on its mystical counterpart.
Translate the cup as mortal poison and gather the classical and historical parallels for it, reduce the four named evils to two, and prefer the third person where the versions support it.
Read the sleep as the stupor of despair rather than of sin, and press the theology of the cup, that where a cup of fornication has been drunk a cup of fury follows.

debates.question: What sleep is Jerusalem told to wake from?

positions.view: the stupor of despair rather than the sleep of sin, as with disciples sleeping for sorrow
death itself, the church rising as the witnesses stood on their feet
a drunken sleep, the call showing that the ruin is not irretrievable
a forlorn condition, simply to be roused and stood upright again

debates.question: Two things are named but four words follow: how do they divide?

positions.view: alternately, desolation by famine and destruction by the sword, the Chaldee paraphrast having missed this and taken refuge in two afflictions now and four to come
two effects and two causes
the affliction itself and the absence of any friend to bear it

debates.question: Who is left to comfort her?

positions.view: read the third person, who shall comfort thee, on the evidence of a manuscript and four versions
keep the first person and let it stand at its worst, even God shown failing, or seeming to fail, to find her a comforter
the search comes back empty, no man being able to comfort or relieve her

outliers.reading: Alone reads the cup as literal poison, recalling the ancient practice of despatching criminals by a draught and Socrates sentenced to the hemlock, and alone furnishes the surrounding classical apparatus, Aeschylus on being intoxicated with passion, Plato's imagined potion that induces fear by the draught, and the historical examples of the conqueror's footstool down to a Roman emperor made to stoop for a Persian king.

themes: Awake, awake, stand up, O Jerusalem, which hast drunk at the hand of the Lord the cup of his fury; thou hast drunken the dregs of the cup of trembling, and wrung them out.
There is none to guide her among all the sons whom she hath brought forth; neither is there any that taketh her by the hand of all the sons that she hath brought up.
These two things are come unto thee; who shall be sorry for thee? desolation, and destruction, and the famine, and the sword: by whom shall I comfort thee?
Thy sons have fainted, they lie at the head of all the streets, as a wild bull in a net: they are full of the fury of the Lord, the rebuke of thy God.
Therefore hear now this, thou afflicted, and drunken, but not with wine:

Thus saith thy Lord the Lord, and thy God that pleadeth the cause of his people, Behold, I have taken out of thine hand the cup of trembling, even the dregs of the cup of my fury; thou shalt no more drink it again:

But I will put it into the hand of them that afflict thee; which have said to thy soul, Bow down, that we may go over: and thou hast laid thy body as the ground, and as the street, to them that went over.
